name: Sara Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead operator on the corrugator at Northgate Packaging. That's the machine that glues paper into cardboard sheets, about a hundred metres long, with steam rollers at one end and a knife at the other. I start at seven, check the glue and the paper reels, and then spend the shift keeping the board flat and the speed up. I like it when the board comes off dead flat all day. I don't like the heat in summer or the noise, even with ear defenders.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up running it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I started as a reel handler at nineteen and just kept asking questions. The old lead, Frank, retired two years ago and picked me to take over, which surprised a few of the men. I'm not a computer person, I go by feel and by the sound of the rollers. My partner Tomas drives lorries for a delivery firm, so between us we keep a modest flat going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I don't use any of that AI stuff anyway, so I wouldn't miss it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that people get carried away with new gadgets. At work I'd shrug and get on with the shift. I'm not one for posting online, so I'd keep it to the break room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI going nowhere doesn't fix our real problem. Box orders are down about 15% this year because online shops are using less packaging. Management already cut Saturday overtime, and that was a good chunk of my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep the corrugator running well, because the best operators are the last to go if there are cuts. I'd keep the £100 a month going into savings, and we'd stop eating out on Fridays. Tomas and I would put off getting a car of our own for another year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, if I'm honest. Not about computers. About the order book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much did losing Saturday overtime cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About £180 a month. That was our holiday money, basically. We managed, but it means we're at about three months of savings instead of five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is Tomas's job steady?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady enough for now. He does supermarket runs, nights mostly. He's heard talk about self-driving lorries, but he says they've been talking about that for ten years.

say: I'd say people get **carried away** with new gadgets.
I'd keep my views to the **break room**, not online.
think: AI stalling doesn't fix our real problem: **falling box orders**, down about 15%.
Losing **Saturday overtime** already cut my pay.
do: Keep the corrugator running **well**, so I'm last to go in cuts.
Keep saving **£100 a month** and stop Friday meals out.
Put off buying a **car** for another year.
feel: **Uneasy** about the **order book**, not about computers.
S0.quote: AI going nowhere doesn't fix our real problem. Box orders are down about 15% this year because online shops are using less packaging.
fieldNote: Her worry here is **ordinary business**: falling orders and lost overtime.
Losing overtime cost her about **£180 a month** and shrank her savings.
She trusts **skill** to protect her, rather than technology.

steps.text: Keep the corrugator running flat and fast every shift
Stop Friday meals out and keep saving £100 a month
Put off buying a car for another year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office bit changes first. Ordering, planning, all that. And then robots for us, just slower. Right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that it's not the end of the world, because the corrugator still needs someone who knows what they're doing. To friends I'd say both sides overdo it, the doom-mongers and the tech lot. Keep calm and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the planning office already does our schedule on a screen, and if that gets cleverer they'll squeeze the machine harder. Then the robots come slowly, but our plant is old, and it's cheaper to build a new robot plant than fix ours. That's what scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see for the first year, honestly, and not go chasing courses. I'd try to push our savings back to five months by cutting the gym and one phone contract. If Northgate started talking about closing, I'd look at the other box plant across town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, underneath. I'd act normal, but I'd be watching every management meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait instead of doing a course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't know which course. Everyone said learn coding ten years ago, and now coding's one of the things going. I'd rather keep my money than spend it on the wrong thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tomas in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the dispatch and routes go to computers, his manager might go, but he still drives. That's the one good thing. For now he's the one with the safer job, which is a strange thought.

say: I'd say it's **not the end** of the world for skilled operators.
I'd tell friends **both sides** exaggerate, so stay calm.
think: Smarter planning means they'll **squeeze the machine** harder.
Our **old plant** might be closed instead of fitted with robots.
do: **Wait and see** for the first year rather than chase courses.
Cut the **gym and one phone** contract to rebuild savings.
Look at the **other box plant** if closure talk starts.
S1.quote: Everyone said learn coding ten years ago, and now coding's one of the things going.
fieldNote: Her real fear is the **old plant closing**, not a robot taking her seat.
She distrusts courses because past **advice** turned out wrong.
She sees her partner's driving as the **safer job** for now.

steps.text: Hold off on paying for any course in the first year
Cancel the gym and one phone contract to save more
Ask about openings at the other box plant across town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. And then robots that can do my job in 2031. And Tomas's lorry too, I'd imagine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government's got to do something quickly, because nobody's ready. At work I'd tell the younger lads to save everything they can. I'm not political, but I'd vote for whoever had an actual plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think we're in real trouble. My job is hands-on, so I'd have until 2031, but my partner Tomas drives a lorry, and a lorry is a robot on wheels. That's both of us by about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every penny, no holidays, no car, and get to six months fast. I'd talk to my mum about moving back in with her if we had to, because she has a spare room in Westbrook. And I'd probably have to swallow my pride and do a course, maybe electrical, because I can't sit and wait for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd wake up at four thinking about it, I know I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym's already gone in the slow one. Here it's the phone contracts, Tomas's football, and any idea of a wedding. We'd been talking about one in 2028. That would wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do a course. You've said you're wary of them. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years changes it. If it's five or ten, I could wait to see what's working. With two, waiting is just losing time I don't have.

say: I'd say the **government** must act fast because nobody is ready.
I'd tell younger workers to **save everything** they can.
think: My job lasts until **2031**, but my partner Tomas drives **lorries**.
Both of our incomes could go by about **2031**.
do: Cut holidays and the car to reach **six months** saved.
Plan to move into **my mum's** spare room if needed.
Start an **electrical course** despite my doubts.
feel: **Frightened**, lying awake at four in the morning.
S2.quote: My job is hands-on, so I'd have until 2031, but my partner Tomas drives a lorry, and a lorry is a robot on wheels.
fieldNote: Both household earners face **robots by 2031**, which drives her fear.
The planned **2028 wedding** would be postponed.
Speed pushes this resistant person towards **retraining** she'd normally avoid.

steps.text: Cut holidays and car plans to reach six months saved
Arrange to move into my mum's spare room in Westbrook if needed
Enrol on an evening electrical course at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots in 2034. That's less of a cliff, but it's still the same cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so let's plan. I'd want the company to tell us straight what it's doing with the plant, and I'd ask that at the staff meeting. I'd say the same to friends: don't panic, but don't pretend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think Northgate closes before 2034. An old plant with an old corrugator, and a new robot plant somewhere cheaper. I'd be about 34 and out of work in a trade that doesn't exist anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or two to see where the jobs actually go, because I don't trust the guesses. Then I'd pick something that needs hands and a licence, like electrician or gas engineer. Tomas and I would get the wedding done cheaply, no big do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy most days, frightened on bad ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you pick electrician over gas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whichever the people who already do it tell me. I'd ask Frank's son, he's an electrician. I trust a person over a website.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year or two. Isn't that risky with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've watched people jump into things and fall flat. I'd rather lose a year than lose my savings on the wrong course.

say: I'd ask management at the staff meeting **straight** what's planned for the plant.
I'd tell friends **don't panic**, but don't pretend.
think: I'd be about **34** with a trade that no longer exists.
do: **Wait a year** or two to see where jobs go.
Then train in a **licensed trade** like electrician.
Hold a **cheap wedding** instead of a big one.
feel: **Uneasy** most days and **frightened** on bad ones.
S3.quote: I'd rather lose a year than lose my savings on the wrong course.
fieldNote: She expects the **plant to close**, so her mood stays high despite more time.
She would take career advice from **people she knows**, not websites.
Her caution shows as a **deliberate delay** before acting.

steps.text: Wait two years to see which trades are hiring
Ask Frank's son about training as an electrician
Hold a small, cheap wedding with Tomas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Robots in 2039. I'd be nearly forty. That feels more manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is something we can deal with, if people use their heads. At work I'd tell people to keep going but keep their eyes open. That's about as much as I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still think the corrugator goes eventually, but I'd have most of a career in front of me afterwards. Ten years of wages and savings helps a lot. I'd be worried, but not like the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the corrugator for five or six years and save hard. Around 2032 I'd start an electrical apprenticeship, the adult route. We'd get married properly and maybe look at buying, if prices stayed where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can live with it. Ten years makes it feel like a problem, not a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start the electrical training earlier than 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw robots going into other box plants. If the place across town got them, I'd know we were next, and I'd start that year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd have time too. He's talked about training as an ambulance driver, which needs a person in the back anyway. We'd both have a plan by then.

say: I'd say we can **deal with it** if people use their heads.
I'd tell colleagues to **keep going** with their eyes open.
think: The corrugator still goes, but I'd have **most of a career** left.
**Ten years** of wages and savings helps a lot.
do: Keep running the corrugator and **save hard** for five years.
Get married and look at **buying a home**.
feel: **Worried but coping**: a problem, not a **disaster**.
S4.quote: Ten years makes it feel like a problem, not a disaster.
fieldNote: She still expects to lose the job, so she stays **anxious**, just steadier.
Her trigger to act is **robots** arriving at a rival plant across town.
Her partner also has a **plan B** as an ambulance driver.

steps.text: Keep running the corrugator and save hard until 2032
Start an adult electrical apprenticeship around 2032
Get married and look at buying a flat with Tomas

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's both of us at once, me and Tomas. What would help is honest notice from Northgate about the plant, and courses that are free and actually lead to a job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old plants. Everyone talks about robots coming in. In our case I think they just shut the old place and build a new one somewhere else. Nobody retrains you for that.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about robots coming in. In our case I think they just shut the old place and build a new one somewhere else.
portrait: Sara is a 27-year-old **lead operator** on a cardboard corrugator who works by feel and sound.
She never uses AI and distrusts **courses** chosen from guesses.
Falling orders make her **uneasy** even in a plateau.
Fast AGI **alarms** her because her partner's lorry driving is exposed too.
Her plan B is a **licensed trade** like electrician, chosen on a trusted person's advice.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her and her partner's **jobs** could both go.
whatWouldHelp: **Free courses** that lead to real jobs.
